extracted.intended_audience: British readers, policymakers, and educated public interested in the French Revolution and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical essay evaluating the proposed French constitution and the political arrangements of the Revolution, arguing principles for how representation, elections, and governmental cohesion ought to be structured. The text lays out normative criteria for constitution-making and for judging the effects of fiscal and monetary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should be a contest between persons/descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The contest between the rich and the poor is not a struggle between corporation and corporation, but a contest between men and men; a competition not between districts, but between descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges or representation intended to favour the wealthy should be conferred on individuals or on classes of rich persons, not on territorial or corporate units; representation must reflect human descriptions (rich/poor) rather than merely territorial corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: If contribution-based favour is intended, confer it on individuals or classes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contrivers of this scheme meant any sort of favour to the rich in consequence of their contribution, they ought to have conferred the privilege either on the individual rich, or on some class formed of rich persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting privilege to a territory (mass) rather than to the contributing individuals produces mismatches between contribution and political advantage; policy should align political privilege with the actual contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invert scheme: equal masses, votes within masses proportioned to property
rubrics_metrics.description: It would answer its purpose better if the scheme were inverted; that the votes of the masses were rendered equal; and that the votes within each mass were proportioned to property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes making mass-level representation equal while apportioning influence within each mass according to property to avoid the dangers of unequal masses and to better reflect contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by contribution is inequitable and impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation, to be measured by contribution, is the most difficult to settle upon principles of equity, in a country which considers its districts as members of a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tax incidence and revenue flows (e.g., import duties paid by scattered consumers, provincial revenues spent in Paris) confound local bases of contribution; using local masses as proxies for contribution yields inequities and is politically unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix inconsistent bases (population, territory, contribution) without coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle which the committee call the basis of population, does not begin to operate from the same point with the two other principles called the bases of territory and of contribution, which are both of an aristocratic nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining multiple bases that operate from different starting points produces absurd inequalities; a constitution must be internally consistent about which basis it uses and how they interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design must account for moral and political realities and human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: In a great arrangement of mankind, not one reference whatsoever is to be found to any thing moral or any thing politic; nothing that relates to the concerns, the actions, the passions, the interests of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators must study human nature, social habits, professions, and local circumstances rather than relying on abstract metaphysics, geometry, or arithmetic when framing constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify citizens by relevant moral/social differences and allot roles/privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislators of antiquity disposed their citizens into such classes, and placed them in such situations in the state, as their peculiar habits might qualify them to fill, and allotted to them such appropriated privileges as might secure what their specific occasions required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper classification (by birth, education, profession, residence, property quality) and tailored political roles/privileges act as indirect restraints against despotism and help a republic endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should be oriented to the whole with a standing authority as centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Each deputy to the Assembly would be the representative of France, and of all its descriptions... This standing, unalterable, fundamental government would make, and it is the only thing which could make, that territory truly and properly a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of sovereign elective assemblies that are the sole centre, there should be a reference government (trustee) that secures unity and equality among districts; representatives should serve the nation, not act as independent sovereign parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid multi-stage elections that sever representatives from the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The member who goes to the National Assembly is not chosen by the people, nor accountable to them. There are three elections before he is chosen ... so as to render him ... an ambassador of a state, and not the representative of the people within a state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interposed magistracies and multiple electoral stages change the spirit of election and produce representatives who are not directly answerable to primary electors; this undermines accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary electors cannot effectively make personal choices or hold representatives accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: What is it we all seek for in an election? To answer its real purposes, you must first possess the means of knowing the fitness of your man; and then you must retain some hold upon him by personal obligation or dependence. Primary electors ... can never know any thing of the qualities of him that is to serve them, nor has he any obligation whatsoever to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegating personal choice in the electoral chain is especially unfit: if electors cannot assess a candidate's fitness nor later enforce accountability, the representative system fails its purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent rotation and re-election ineligibility undermine competence and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man who has served in an assembly is ineligible for two years after. Just as these magistrates begin to learn their trade, like chimney-sweepers, they are disqualified for exercising it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short terms combined with enforced breaks prevent representatives from acquiring experience and continuity, producing superficial, interrupted, and ineffective governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking a country into independent republics without constitutional cohesion is dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: This scheme has a direct and immediate tendency to sever France into a variety of republics, and to render them totally independent of each other, without any direct constitutional means of coherence, connexion, or subordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decentralization without standing authority or constitutional mechanisms of coherence risks fragmentation, lack of concerted policy, and possibly conflict among the resulting entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confiscation plus compulsory paper currency as 'cement' will produce oligarchy and instability
rubrics_metrics.description: The confiscation, with the compulsory paper currency annexed to it ... may for some time compose some sort of cement ... but ... it will add infinitely to the dissociation, distraction, and confusion... One thing only is certain ... its effect in producing an oligarchy in every one of the republics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A paper circulation not founded on real money and supported by confiscation concentrates power in the hands of managers and speculators, ties revenue to credit fluctuations, and destabilizes political cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning land into a speculative asset via paper and sales harms agriculture and local stability
rubrics_metrics.description: This continual exchanging land for paper ... the spirit of money-jobbing and speculation goes into the mass of land itself ... That species of property becomes, as it were, volatilized; it assumes an unnatural and monstrous activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selling confiscated land into a paper-based market converts stable landed property into a volatile commodity, encouraging speculation over productive agriculture and eroding local rootedness.
